overview: Sibir was a western Siberian khanate connecting forest, river and steppe communities. This atlas shows 1492 to 1600, not its complete political lifetime. Its nearly unchanged outline cannot track shifting tribute relationships, expansion or conquest. Turkic-speaking Tatars, Khanty and Mansi belonged to different communities within its changing reach.

periods.title: Rival ruling families
periods.summary: The atlas opens during the transition from Chimgi-Tura toward Isker under the Taybugids.

periods.title: Kuchum takes power
periods.summary: A Shaybanid ruler challenges regional rivals and Moscow.

periods.title: Conquest and resistance
periods.summary: Isker falls; fighting and negotiations continue.

items.text: The khanate emerged from the breakup of the Golden Horde. Chimgi-Tura, at present-day Tyumen, was an earlier seat. In the 1490s the Taybugid dynasty shifted its center to Isker, also called Sibir. Kuchum, from a rival Shaybanid line claiming descent from Chinggis Khan, seized power in 1563.

Local life depended on fishing, hunting, livestock, cultivation and skilled metalworking. Trade brought textiles, carpets, ornaments and medicines from Central Asia, while furs and hunting birds traveled outward. Siberian households participated in networks reaching Kazan, the Nogai steppe and Russia.

A message could be an object. Chronicles describe Kuchum summoning followers by sending gilded arrows. Tataurov compares this account with large decorated arrowheads from Isker and proposes a signaling function. The connection is an interpretation: a fancy arrowhead does not come with its original delivery instructions.

Seals helped make authority visible. Large signet rings found at western Siberian sites carry designs including tamgas, faces or mounted warriors. A Russian rendering of Kuchum’s 1571 oath says he attached his seal. An official could authenticate a promise with an object small enough to wear.

sections.title: Making a home and a living

items.text: At Isker, keys and chest handles survive among objects assigned to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Researchers connect the chests with safekeeping important possessions. We cannot open them to discover a family’s treasures, but the hardware preserves the familiar business of putting something away and locking it up.

The same collections include bone awls, unfinished bone objects and a spoon handle. These small pieces bring cutting, piercing and making utensils into the picture beside all the weapons. Bone could become a useful tool or part of a meal’s equipment, rather than simply being thrown away.

Regional potters mixed crushed old pottery into clay and pressed rows of dents or comb-like impressions over their vessels. Many pots had rounded bottoms. At Tunus, a sixteenth-century layer contains several ceramic traditions together: even a collection of broken dinnerware can preserve evidence of neighbors with different habits.

Isker’s objects also include Chinese bronze mirrors, beads, jewelry and painted porcelain fragments. These imports suggest access to valued goods through long-distance exchange. Some people could look into a metal mirror and use dishes that had traveled much farther than they had; those luxuries were not every household’s possessions.

Adamov’s 2021 study identifies evidence for blacksmiths, metal casters, jewelers, tailors and leatherworkers at Isker. Silver and copper coins also occur. A royal center needed people repairing clothing, working hides and making everyday objects as well as warriors and rulers; the author argues for a substantial resident community.

Some royal children and grandchildren had tutors called atalyks. These men also performed diplomatic missions and collected tribute. The same person might look after a prince’s upbringing and then leave on government business. This is evidence about the ruling household, not a school system available to every child.

During negotiations in 1597, Kuchum requested medicines seized with a Bukhara caravan. He wanted their return as a test of Russian promises. The account reveals remedies moving along trade routes, but does not identify their ingredients or demonstrate whether they worked.

A real voice survives through translation. Kuchum’s 1597 letter says, in the preserved Russian wording: “а Сибирь не яз отдал, сами естя взяли”. Transliterated: a Sibir ne yaz otdal, sami estya vzyali. It means “I did not give up Siberia; you took it yourselves.” This is an archaic Russian rendering quoted by historians, not the khan’s original Tatar script or a sample of everybody’s speech.

How did letters cross languages? A March 1570 official report records a letter from Kuchum written in Tatar and separately mentions sending its translation to Ivan IV. Couriers, readers and translators made diplomacy possible. The source itself reminds us that the language preserved in an archive may differ from the language first written.

The Irtysh has eroded Isker, and early souvenir collecting scattered finds and destroyed their contexts. Tataurov and Tataurov questioned whether it was a permanent capital. Adamov’s later study argues for a resident town using its substantial deposits, fortifications and craft evidence. Archaeologists disagree over the settlement’s scale and character.

Adamov reports that the late-fifteenth-century settlement covered at least 2.6 hectares and had a complex system of defenses. Large bricks found in 2019 suggest masonry buildings, although that is a proposal rather than a recovered palace plan. A small surviving site can conceal a much larger landscape lost to a river.

Not everything found at Isker belonged to the khans. Adamov’s 2020 study identified at least twenty vessel rims, a clay spindle whorl and three bronze fittings that may belong to the sixth- to ninth-century Potchevash culture. A spindle whorl helps turn fibers into thread. These objects illuminate earlier inhabitants, centuries before Kuchum.

An official list dated 4 September 1598 names members of Kuchum’s captured household, including children aged five and six. The military defeat reached families as well as soldiers. Such lists record people through their captors’ administration; the young prisoners were real children, not just entries in a victory report.
Siberian Tatar communities continued after the khanate’s loss of independence and live in western Siberia today.

ending.text: Muscovite conquest continued after Isker’s capture. Kuchum was defeated in 1598 but remained free afterward. The atlas’s 1600 seam does not mark a single surrender by every community.
